messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 73

**Vignette: The Unfinished Wireframe**

He describes the beginning not as a moment of collapse, but as a slow, creeping error in the system. For three weeks in the spring of last year, Sam felt a persistent ache in his right side, a dull throb he initially dismissed as a muscle strain from his standing desk or poor posture during late-night coding sessions. He was a UX designer for a large health-tech firm, and his life was a series of user flows, journey maps, and iterative fixes. He figured he could debug his own body with enough sleep and ibuprofen.

The diagnosis arrived on a Tuesday. Stage II colorectal cancer. The doctor’s words felt like a corrupted file—fragmented, unreadable. Sam remembers the fluorescent light in the exam room buzzing at a frequency that seemed to vibrate in his teeth. He remembers his wife, Lin, squeezing his hand so hard her knuckles went white. He remembers thinking, *This is a terrible interface for bad news.*

The treatment was brutal. Surgery to remove the tumor, followed by six months of chemotherapy. He lost forty pounds. He lost his hair. He lost the ability to work, which for Sam was not just a job but a framework for his identity. He spent his days on the couch, watching the shadows of leaves move across the ceiling, feeling his body betray him like a faulty prototype. The chemo fog was thick; he could not focus on a single line of code. He felt like a ghost haunting his own home.

That was fourteen months ago. The scans are clean now. The doctors use words like "remission" and "excellent prognosis." Sam is back at work, but something is fundamentally broken in his operating system.

He cannot stop checking for errors. Every morning, he wakes in a cold sweat at 4:17 AM—the exact time his first chemo infusion began. His heart races as he runs a full system diagnostic on his body: he presses on his abdomen, feels for lumps, analyzes the color of his urine, the texture of his skin. If his stomach gurgles, he freezes, certain the cancer has returned and metastasized. This is not a rational thought; it is a reflex. He spends forty-five minutes a day in the bathroom, conducting these silent, terrified audits.

At the office, his performance has cratered. He used to be known for his intuitive, fluid designs. Now, he cannot make a decision. He stares at a blank Figma canvas for hours, paralyzed by the fear of a single wrong click. A minor bug in a prototype sends him into a spiral of catastrophic thinking: *This is the end. This error will ruin the launch. I will be fired. We will lose our health insurance. I will get sick again and die.* He has started leaving meetings abruptly, claiming he has a headache, just to escape the pressure of a normal conversation. The sound of a colleague coughing near his desk makes him flinch; he immediately reaches for the hand sanitizer in his pocket.

He has not touched his wife in months. Not because he does not love her, but because intimacy feels like a vulnerability he cannot afford. Sex reminds him that he has a body, and his body is a source of terror. He sleeps in the guest room now, curled on his side, the door slightly ajar so he can see the hallway light. He needs to know he can get to the bathroom quickly if the nausea comes back—even though the nausea has been gone for nearly a year.

Last week, his boss gently suggested he take a leave of absence. Sam nodded, but inside he felt a familiar, crushing weight. He is thirty-five years old. He survived. But survival, he is learning, is not the same as being alive. He feels like a wireframe with no content—a structure that is perfectly clean, but utterly empty.
